Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 88, verse 1–7:

﴿Has the overwhelming event reached you?﴾ This is an interrogative used to draw attention and to magnify the matter. It was said that "hal" here means "qad" (indeed), but this view is weak. ﴿Al-ghashiyah﴾ (the overwhelming) is the Resurrection, because it overwhelms all creation. It was also said that it is the Fire, based on His words: ﴿and the Fire will cover their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50]. This view is weak, because after it He mentions two groups: the people of wretchedness and the people of happiness. ﴿Humbled﴾ means abased. ﴿Labouring and weary﴾: "naṣiba" is from "naṣab," meaning fatigue. Regarding who is meant by them, there are three opinions. The first is that they are the disbelievers. According to this, their labour and weariness may refer to this world, since they used to do evil deeds and exert themselves in them; or it may refer to the Hereafter, where they will labour at things that exhaust them, such as dragging chains and shackles and the like, which adds to their punishment. The second is that it refers to monks who strive hard in worship but whose worship is not accepted, because they are not upon Islam. Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) interpreted it this way, and he wept out of pity for a Christian monk whom he saw striving hard. According to this, "labouring and weary" refers to this world, and "weary" points to their exertion in works that will not benefit them, so they have nothing from it but fatigue. The third is that it refers to the Qadariyyah. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the Qadariyyah and wept, and said: "Among them are the diligent."

﴿They will be given to drink from a boiling spring﴾, i.e., one that is extremely hot. From the same root is ﴿a scorching hot water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. The form of "aniyah" here is "fa'ilah," unlike "aniyah min fiddah" (vessels of silver), whose form is "af'ilah."

﴿They will have no food except from a thorny plant (dari')﴾. Regarding "dari'," there are four opinions. The first is that it is a thorn called al-shibraq, which is a deadly poison. This is the most preferred of the opinions, because the lexicographers mentioned it, and because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ad-dari' is a thorn in the Fire." The second is that it is al-zaqqum, based on His words: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum is the food of the sinner﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43-44]. The third is that it is a green, foul-smelling plant that grows in the sea. This is weak, because what flows in a valley is not food but drink. How excellent is the saying of the one who said: "Ad-dari' is the food of the people of the Fire," for it is more general and safer from the obligation of specifying. Some derive its etymology from "mudari'ah," meaning resemblance, because it resembles good food while not being so. It was also said that it means "mudarri'" (that which emaciates the body), i.e., weakening it. It was also said that the Arabs do not know this word. If it is asked: how does He say here, "They will have no food except from dari'," while in al-Haqqah He says, "and no food except from ghassalin"? The answer: the dari' is for one group and the ghassalin is for another group, or one applies in one state and the other in another state.

﴿Neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾: this clause is an attribute of "dari'," and it negates from "food" the benefit of food, which is nourishing and relieving hunger.

﴿Faces that Day will be blissful﴾, meaning enjoying delight in the Garden, or the radiance of bliss will appear upon them. ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾, meaning pleased in the Hereafter because of their striving, which is their deeds in this world. ﴿In a lofty Garden﴾. It may be lofty in place, or lofty in rank, or both. ﴿Where they hear no idle talk﴾. It is from *laghw* (idle or vain speech), and its meaning is obscenity and what is disliked. It may mean "no idle word" or "no idle group." ﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾. It may mean the category of springs, or one particular spring which He honoured by specifying it. ﴿And cups set in place﴾. Cups have already been mentioned. *Mawḍūʿah* means present and prepared with their drinks. In His saying "raised up" and "set in place" there is *muṭābaqah* (antithesis). ﴿And cushions﴾, the plural of *namruqah* (*namāriq*), which is the pillow. ﴿And carpets spread out﴾. These are luxurious spreads. It is said they are *ṭanāfis* (sing. *ṭunfusah*), and their singular is *zarbiyyah* (*zarābī*). ﴿Spread out﴾ means scattered, which is an expression of their abundance. It is also said it means laid out flat. ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ This is an exhortation to reflect on their creation, because of the wonders in their strength, their submission to every weak person, their patience with thirst, and the many benefits in them: riding, carrying loads, eating their meat, drinking their milk, their urine, and other things. It is also said that by "camels" is meant the clouds, but this is far-fetched; the one who said it was prompted by their connection to the sky, the earth and the mountains. The correct view is that the intended meaning is the well-known animal. It was mentioned because of the wonders in it, and because the Arabs took care of it, since their livelihood was mostly from it, and it was the most numerous of livestock in their lands.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 88, verses 22–25:

﴿You are not over them a controller.﴾ That is, a compeller, one who holds power over them. This is among the abrogated (mansukh) rulings, abrogated by the sword. ﴿Except for those who turn away﴾ is an exceptive clause that is disjunctive (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but as for those who turn away ﴿and disbelieve, * Allah will punish them﴾. It has also been said that it is an exception from the object that has been omitted (istithna' min mafu'l fa-dhukira), and the meaning is: remind everyone, except those who turn away, until you despair of them; on this view the exception is connected (muttasil). It has also been said that it is an exception from the statement ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾, meaning: you have power only over those who turn away and disbelieve, and on this view it is connected and there is no abrogation in it, since there is no truce (muwada'ah) in it. This view is weak, because the surah is Meccan and the truce (muwada'ah) at Makkah is established. ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾, that is, their return, and the verse is a threat.
